articleHeadline: Heat Erodes Wolbachia Shield Against Dengue in Mosquitoes, Study Finds
articleSummary: Vietnamese laboratory study shows elevated rearing temperature weakens Wolbachia (wMel)-mediated protection against dengue virus (DENV) in Aedes aegypti. articleSummary: Malaria control using attractive targeted sugar baits (ATSB) with Westham Sarabi v1.2 failed to reduce malaria in three large Phase III trials conducted in Kenya, Mali, and Zambia. articleSummary: In a retrospective Chinese study of 519 children hospitalized with symptomatic SARS-CoV-2 infection (Dec 2022–Dec 2025), 345 (66.4%) were infants or toddlers. articleSummary: Dengue knowledge among frontline nurses in Indonesia improves more with a board game than lectures in a cluster randomized trial. articleSummary: Plague (Yersinia pestis) in Vietnam presents in three forms—bubonic, septicemic, and pneumonic. articleSummary: Group A Streptococcus (GAS) infection can cause streptococcal pharyngitis (strep throat), impetigo, and serious downstream complications. In children, especially ages 5–15, strep throat presents with abrupt fever, sore throat, painful swallowing, red tonsils with pus, tender cervical nodes, plus headaches and fatigue; some cases include nausea, abdominal pain, or rash. Prompt testing (rapid GAS antigen or throat culture) is recommended; skin infections are diagnosed by lesion appearance and exam. If untreated, GAS pharyngitis may trigger acute rheumatic fever (1–5 weeks later) with carditis, migratory polyarthritis, Sydenham chorea, erythema marginatum, and subcutaneous nodules, risking chronic rheumatic heart disease. Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis may follow throat or skin infection, presenting with dark urine, periorbital edema, hypertension, reduced urine output. Streptococcal toxic shock syndrome is rare but life-threatening, requiring urgent hospitalization. Antibiotic therapy as prescribed by a clinician is key to prevention.

articleHeadline: Computational Models Warn Ebola Antibody Drugs May Lose Power Against
articleSummary: During the 2026 Bundibugyo virus disease outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Uganda, researchers assessed whether existing Ebola antibody therapies would work against Bundibugyo virus (BDBV). Analyzing 44 BDBV glycoprotein sequences, including 12 from the outbreak, they mapped substitutions onto epitopes of leading therapeutics using structural modelling and AlphaFold to predict effects on antibody–antigen binding. For mAb114 (Ebanga), mutations E112D and P116A fall within its epitope and are predicted to weaken binding and substantially reduce affinity, potentially compromising efficacy. For Inmazeb (atoltivimab, maftivimab, odesivimab), odesivimab preserves its epitope, while atoltivimab and maftivimab alone fail to bind; the complete cocktail shows synergistic binding, possibly preserving activity. MBP134, a two-antibody combination, offers the clearest optimism. The work underscores the urgent need for real-time genomic surveillance to guide therapy choices during active outbreaks.

articleSummary: First three-dimensional structure of a TenpIN toxin–antitoxin system, a type III bacterial anti-phage defense found in major pathogens such as Salmonella enterica, Shigella flexneri, Klebsiella pneumoniae and Escherichia coli. articleHeadlineTranslated: Is pneumonia in children contagious?
articleHeadline: Viêm phổi ở trẻ có lây?
articleSummary: Contagiousness of pediatric pneumonia depends on cause: viral or bacterial pneumonia spreads via respiratory droplets; pneumonia from aspiration or chemicals is not contagious. Common pathogens include viruses such as RSV, influenza, parainfluenza, metapneumovirus, and adenovirus; and bacteria such as Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Moraxella catarrhalis, and Mycoplasma pneumoniae. Transmission occurs via droplets and indirect contact with hands, toys, and surfaces. Contagion window varies: bacterial pneumonia often becomes less contagious after 24–48 hours of appropriate antibiotics and fever resolution; viral pneumonia remains contagious during acute symptoms. No fixed isolation period. Return to school after fever-free for at least 24 hours without antipyretics and the child is well. Prevention includes handwashing, coughing hygiene, masks in public, not sharing utensils, cleaning surfaces, ventilation; vaccination against influenza, pneumococcus, Hib. Seek care for high fever or worsening breathing. Do not self-prescribe antibiotics. BS.CKII Bùi Thị Khuyên, Pediatrics, Tam Anh Clinic Cau Giay, Hanoi.

articleSummary: Rising rodent infestations across Taiwan raise concern about plague (Yersinia pestis). The disease spreads to humans mainly by rat fleas or direct contact with infected animals and occurs in three forms: pneumonic plague (airborne droplets, up to 2 m, 1–3 day incubation), bubonic plague (lymph node swelling, 2–6 day incubation), and septicemic plague (blood infection with fever, bleeding; possible limb necrosis). Antibiotics such as aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, and doxycycline for 10–14 days are essential; bubonic cases with abscessed nodes may require drainage. No effective vaccine exists; prevention focuses on avoiding flea bites and reducing contact with potentially infected animals and rodents. Globally (2019–2025), 3,860 suspected, 2,646 confirmed, 423 deaths; Congo DR and Madagascar are hotspots; Taiwan last had plague in 1953. WHO assessments call the Irkutsk, Russia case low public health risk.
